newsitem.title: UK: More jobs in UK finance, 1st rise since '95 - CBI.
newsitem.headline: More jobs in UK finance, 1st rise since '95 - CBI.

text.p: Employment in Britain's financial services sector is on the increase for the first time since September 1995, according to a survey released on Monday.

The survey by top employers group the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and Coopers and Lybrand said the rise in financial services jobs over the three months to March, was a response to buoyant demand.

"(This) reflects continuing strength in the capital markets sector and expansion of distribution capability in retail financial services, in response to more buoyant demand," said Pat Newberry, Coopers and Lybrand consulting practice partner.

Out of 302 firms polled, 38 said they had increased the number of jobs, while 27 reduced them, leaving a positive balance of 11 percent. This compared with negative balances of nine percent in December and 29 in March 1996.

The survey showed business optimism increased for the fifth time in a row, although the rise was the slowest since December 1995. It also noted that higher profitability was expected over the next three months.

CBI chief economic adviser Kate Barker said the results were encouraging, but added: "The survey does indicate a reduced tempo of growth, with a slight rise in the level of demand as a constraint on business over the coming year."
Securities traders and life insurers saw the largest increase in business optmism with only general insurers noting a fall in confidence.
In the retail sector, Newberry said a further wave of mergers was likely because of over-capacity and a growing tendency for customers to shop around.

Despite the improvement in employment, cost pressures will remain intense as firms step up spending on advertising and keep investing in information technology to develop efficient delivery and customer inflation systems, Newberry added.
Barker attempted to allay fears that Britain's buoyant economy may lead to an explosion in inflation, saying Britain could get away with a year of strong growth.
"There is scope to grow above trend for a year without causing problems for inflation," she told Reuters.

Speaking ahead of the monthly monetary meeting between Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Thursday, Barker said the question of interest rates was a difficult one at the moment.
"In every sector competitive conditions are very tight. There is still a lot of cost cutting around."
Asked whether the UK could afford to wait and see before raising its 6.0 percent base interest rate, she replied "yes."
